summary: Describes authentication methods and security mechanisms for LDAP. It covers using StartTLS to set up TLS, simple bind (anonymous, unauthenticated and name/password), SASL bind including EXTERNAL, and the authentication and authorization states of a session. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: How the address-book server checks who you are before it lets you in, from a guest pass to a real password, and how to make the line private.

questions: what is the difference between anonymous and unauthenticated ldap bind
how does sasl work in ldap
subtitle: How LDAP clients prove who they are and protect the connection: StartTLS, simple Bind and SASL.

tldr.problem: LDAP directories face threats from hostile clients and from attackers on the network path, and implementations need a common minimum set of security functions to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4513 defines the StartTLS operation for TLS, the simple Bind method (anonymous, unauthenticated and name/password) and the SASL Bind method including EXTERNAL, and describes the authorization state of a session.
tldr.outcome: It sets the mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms for LDAP and obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2829 and RFC 2830. It has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4513 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2251, RFC 2829 and RFC 2830, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Threats and Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP, RFC 4510) is used to search, retrieve and change directory content. The RFC lists eight basic threats, including unauthorized access to or modification of directory data, theft of reusable client credentials by monitoring, denial of service, spoofing and session hijacking.

LDAP offers authentication through the Bind operation, integrity and confidentiality through TLS or SASL security layers, server authentication, and administrative resource limits. It offers no standard access control facility, only mechanisms to support vendor-specific ones. The RFC argues that letting implementations pick and choose mechanisms does not lead to interoperability, so it mandates a minimum set.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory can be spied on, tampered with, or tricked by impostors. This RFC lists the dangers and the locks LDAP gives you.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
LDAP servers MUST support the anonymous mechanism of the simple Bind method. Any implementation that supports an authentication mechanism other than anonymous MUST support the name/password mechanism of simple Bind and MUST be able to protect it with TLS established by StartTLS. Implementations SHOULD disallow name/password authentication by default when suitable data security is not in place.

Servers SHOULD support the SASL EXTERNAL mechanism. Implementations that support TLS MUST support the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA ciphersuite and SHOULD support TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, the latter to ease interoperability with earlier LDAP StartTLS specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Every server must at least let guests in. If it lets anyone in with a password, it must also know how to wrap the connection in a privacy tunnel first.

sections.title: The StartTLS Operation
sections.content:
StartTLS, defined in RFC 4511, sets up TLS (RFC 4346) inside an existing LDAP session. A client may send it at any time except when TLS is already established, when a multi-stage SASL negotiation is in progress, or when responses to earlier requests are still outstanding. A detected violation returns operationsError. A client that will both Bind and use StartTLS SHOULD do StartTLS first, so the Bind messages are protected.

To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, the client MUST verify the server's identity against the certificate, normally by comparing the name it connected to with the certificate's subjectAltName values. A wildcard (the asterisk character) is allowed only as the left-most DNS label, so a certificate for the wildcard label under example.com matches a.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com. Using the Common Name is existing practice but deprecated. If the check fails, automated clients SHOULD close the connection.

After TLS is installed, the client SHOULD discard or refresh server information it did not obtain securely, since a man-in-the-middle could have altered it. Both sides should judge whether the resulting security level is adequate and remove the TLS layer if not.
sections.plainLanguage: StartTLS is like putting the phone call into a sealed tube partway through. Before talking secrets, you check that the person at the other end is really who you meant to call.

sections.title: Authorization State
sections.content:
Every LDAP session has an authorization state: what authentication has been established, how, and what security services are in place. Authorization in LDAP is a local matter, and a key factor is the authorization identity.

A new session starts with an anonymous authorization identity, so a client need not Bind first, and the server MUST treat early requests as if they followed an anonymous Bind. When a Bind request arrives, the server immediately moves the session to anonymous. If the Bind succeeds, the session moves to the requested state; otherwise it stays anonymous. Events such as setting up or closing data security services, or an expired certificate, can also return the session to anonymous.
sections.plainLanguage: When you walk in you are treated as a guest. Each time you try to show ID you become a guest again until the check passes.

sections.title: Simple Bind
sections.content:
The simple Bind method has three mechanisms. Anonymous: a zero-length name and a zero-length password. Unauthenticated: a non-empty DN with a zero-length password, which still yields an anonymous state; the DN is only for tracing and logging and must not be validated or used for authorization. Name/password: a non-empty DN and a non-empty password, which yields an authenticated state if the server accepts it.

Unauthenticated Bind is easy to trigger by accident, for example when a user leaves the password empty, and a server may return success for it. Clients SHOULD require the user to choose it by some means other than an empty password, SHOULD refuse an empty password in a name/password interface, and servers SHOULD by default fail such requests with unwillingToPerform.

For name/password, the result code invalidDNSyntax means the DN is malformed, invalidCredentials means the DN or password is not valid, and success means the credentials are valid. The mechanism is not suitable in environments without confidentiality protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A guest pass has no name. A name with no password is just a name tag. Only a name plus the right password gets real access.

sections.title: SASL Bind
sections.content:
The sasl method lets LDAP use any SASL mechanism (RFC 4422). The SASL service name is ldap. A SASL Bind uses BindRequest version 3 with the sasl choice and the mechanism name, and an optional initial response in the credentials field.

Many mechanisms need several round trips. The server sends a challenge in a BindResponse with result code saslBindInProgress, and the client replies with a new BindRequest using the same mechanism. Challenges and responses are opaque binary tokens, not Base64. The exchange ends when the server returns a result other than saslBindInProgress. Security layers take effect after the final successful BindResponse, and a SASL layer sits on top of any TLS layer.

Clients can read supportedSASLMechanisms from the root DSE. Servers SHOULD let all clients read it before and after authentication, so downgrade attacks can be detected. A SASL authorization identity is written either as dn: followed by a distinguished name or u: followed by a user id.

With the EXTERNAL mechanism, the server uses credentials from a lower layer such as a TLS client certificate. With no credentials in the request (implicit assertion) the identity is derived from them; with credentials (explicit assertion) the value is the identity the client asks for. If no lower-layer credentials exist, the Bind MUST fail with inappropriateAuthentication.
sections.plainLanguage: SASL is a plug-in socket for many kinds of ID checks. The server may ask a few questions, and the client answers each, until the server is satisfied or says no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A session without integrity and privacy protection (via StartTLS, IPsec or a suitable SASL mechanism) is open to man-in-the-middle attacks that read and change data. Clients and servers should be configurable to require these protections. StartTLS adds no security by itself; the result depends on TLS and how it is used, and an attacker can remove StartTLS from the root DSE's supportedExtension list, so both parties should check the level achieved.

Name/password Bind discloses the password to the server. Servers that accept cleartext passwords MUST support a policy that requires a TLS layer or other confidentiality protection, or else returns confidentialityRequired, even when the password is right. Mechanisms like DIGEST-MD5 send a hash that may be open to offline dictionary attacks and should also be protected.

Until integrity protection is installed, an attacker can alter the list of SASL mechanisms to leave only the weakest. A client can fetch the list again after integrity protection starts and, if it now shows a stronger mechanism, should reconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Without the sealed tube, anyone along the way can read your password or change the answers. Send secrets only after the tube is in place, and double-check which locks the server really offers.
